units.title: Imperfect Competition
units.description: Analyze market structures where firms have market power, exploring the strategic interactions, pricing strategies, and resulting welfare losses of monopolies, oligopolies, and monopolistically competitive markets.

lectures.title: Market Power and Monopoly
lectures.description: Examine monopolies, analyzing why they have market power, how they maximize profits, and why they cause market inefficiencies.

sessions.title: Market Structures and Barriers to Entry
sessions.description: Define market power and review the sources of barriers to entry that allow monopolies to exist, including legal protections, control of resources, and natural monopolies.
sessions.sessionOutline:
Begin the session on the whiteboard by drawing a simple spectrum of competition. On one extreme, write 'Perfect Competition' and remind students of the key assumption from Unit 3: firms are price takers with zero market power. On the opposite extreme, write 'Monopoly' and introduce the concept of market power as the ability of a single firm to influence the market price of its product. To make this intuitive, ask the students to contrast a local wheat farmer with a local utility provider; the farmer has to accept the going market price, while the utility provider has the unique ability to raise prices without losing all of their customers. This ability to set prices—being a 'price maker'—is the core definition of market power, and it forms the foundation of everything we will study in Unit 4.

Transition to the mechanism that makes a monopoly possible in the first place: barriers to entry. Explain that in perfect competition, positive economic profits attract new firms until profits are driven to zero. For a monopoly to persist in the long run, there must be strong barriers preventing competitors from entering the market. Draw three main categories on the board: Control of Key Resources, Legal/Government Barriers, and Natural Monopolies. Use relatable real-world examples for each. For instance, explain how controlling a unique physical resource (like historical diamond mines or rare mineral deposits) completely shuts out potential competitors from the very beginning. Then, discuss legal barriers such as patents and copyrights, framing them as a deliberate government tradeoff: we grant a temporary monopoly to incentivize innovation, knowing that the inventor can charge a higher price in the short run to recoup research costs.

Deepen the analysis by focusing on the most analytically complex barrier: the Natural Monopoly. Draw a large graph on the board with Quantity on the horizontal axis and Costs/Price on the vertical axis. Sketch a continuously declining Average Total Cost (ATC) curve that sloped downward across the entire relevant range of market demand. This visual representation is crucial for correcting a common student pitfall: many believe natural monopolies are granted by governments because they represent 'essential services' like water or electricity. Clarify that a natural monopoly is actually defined by its cost structure. When a firm experiences massive economies of scale—high fixed setup costs combined with low marginal costs—a single firm can produce the entire market demand at a lower average cost than two or more smaller firms could. Sketching a second, hypothetical scenario with two smaller firms operating at higher points on the ATC curve will visually lock this concept in.

Conclude the whiteboard session with an active practice prompt to test student intuition on these entry barriers. Ask students to analyze a scenario where a local municipality is deciding whether to lay down a second set of sewage pipes to foster competition in waste management. Guide them to see that duplicating the infrastructure would double the fixed costs and force both providers to operate at a much higher average total cost, showing why a single, regulated natural monopolist is the economically logical outcome. This exercise helps students connect the abstract declining ATC curve with real-world infrastructure choices, preparing them to seamlessly transition to calculating monopoly pricing and revenue curves in the next session.

tasks: Identify various barriers to entry in monopolistic markets.
Explain how a natural monopoly arises due to economies of scale over the entire range of market demand.

sessions.title: Monopoly Output and Pricing
sessions.description: Explain why a single-price monopolist's Marginal Revenue (MR) is less than its Price (P). Graph and calculate the monopolist's profit-maximizing output and price.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin this whiteboard session by bridging the concept of market power from the previous session to the concrete financial reality of a monopolist. Unlike a perfectly competitive firm that can sell any quantity at the market-determined price, a monopolist faces the entire downward-sloping market demand curve. This means the monopolist faces a fundamental trade-off: to sell a higher quantity, they must lower their price. The teacher should sketch a simple downward-sloping line labeled 'Demand' and contrast this with the flat, perfectly elastic demand curve of a price-taker, setting up the intuitive foundation that the monopolist is a price-maker who cannot simply set both price and quantity independently.

Next, the teacher will illustrate why Marginal Revenue (MR) is always below Price (P) for a single-price monopolist using a dynamic whiteboard derivation. Let's write out a simple scenario: selling 1 unit at $10 yields $10 in total revenue. To sell 2 units, the price must drop to $9. Total revenue becomes $18. The marginal revenue of that second unit is only $8, which is less than the price of $9. On the whiteboard, decompose this change into the 'Quantity Effect' (gaining $9 from the new sale) and the 'Price Effect' (losing $1 on the first unit). This visually demonstrates the price penalty: because the monopolist must lower the price on all units sold to sell one more, the extra revenue gained is always less than the price charged for that marginal unit. The teacher should then draw the MR curve starting at the same vertical intercept as the demand curve but sloping downward twice as steeply, cementing this mathematical relationship visually.

From this graphical foundation, we introduce the critical relationship between demand elasticity and the Total Revenue curve. Directly beneath the standard price/quantity graph, the teacher should draw a second aligned graph showing Total Revenue (TR) on the vertical axis and quantity on the horizontal axis. As quantity increases in the elastic region of the demand curve, MR is positive, and TR rises. At the exact quantity where MR crosses the horizontal axis (MR = 0), the demand curve is unit-elastic, and TR reaches its peak. Past this point, in the inelastic region, MR is negative, and TR falls. This visual alignment helps students intuitively grasp why a rational monopolist will never choose to produce a quantity in the inelastic portion of their demand curve—because doing so means that increasing output actually reduces total revenue while simultaneously adding to production costs.

Finally, we bring the Marginal Cost (MC) curve onto the whiteboard to determine the firm's profit-maximizing output and price. The teacher should trace the MC curve cutting through the MR curve. We emphasize the golden rule: find the quantity where MR equals MC. A major pitfall for students is the temptation to read the price directly from this intersection point. The teacher must actively combat this by drawing a dashed vertical line from the MR=MC intersection up to the Demand curve, and then tracing horizontally over to the vertical axis to find the monopoly price. This visual routine—'Go to MR=MC, look down for quantity, look up to Demand for price'—prevents the common exam error of pricing at the MC level and ensures students understand that the market's willingness to pay ultimately dictates the monopolist's markup.

tasks: Graph a monopoly demand curve and its corresponding MR curve, demonstrating the relationship between elasticity and the total revenue curve.
Find the profit-maximizing price and output from a monopoly graph.

sessions.title: Monopoly Profit and Economic Inefficiency
sessions.description: Evaluate monopoly outcomes compared to perfect competition, showing how monopolies create deadweight loss, reduce consumer surplus, and fail both allocative and productive efficiency.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin this session by setting up a side-by-side logical comparison on the whiteboard between the gold standard of market performance—perfect competition—and the restrictive reality of a single-price monopoly. The key conceptual goal is to show students that market structure directly dictates societal welfare. We start by drawing a standard market demand curve, explaining that under perfect competition, the industry produces where supply (which is the sum of marginal costs) equals demand, achieving allocative efficiency where marginal benefit exactly equals marginal cost. By establishing this competitive baseline first, students can visually anchor the socially optimal price and quantity before we layer on the distortion of monopoly power.

Next, we introduce the monopoly's pricing and output decisions on the same graph to illustrate the contraction of trade. Under monopoly, the firm restricts output to the point where marginal revenue equals marginal cost, and then charges the highest price consumers are willing to pay on the demand curve. This visual juxtaposition immediately reveals that the monopolist's price is higher and its quantity is lower than the competitive ideal. We will guide the teacher to physically trace the loss of consumer surplus on the board, demonstrating how a portion of what used to be consumer welfare is transferred directly to the monopolist as producer surplus, while another portion vanishes entirely from the market. This missing economic value represents the deadweight loss.

A major pitfall for students here is incorrectly shading the deadweight loss area. They often mistakenly draw a rectangle or shade the entire area between demand and marginal cost up to the vertical axis. To prevent this, the lesson script guides the teacher to emphasize the 'lost transactions' intuition: deadweight loss is a triangle pointing to the right, bound by the demand curve on top (marginal benefit), the marginal cost curve on the bottom, and restricted by the monopoly quantity on the left and the competitive quantity on the right. We walk through a quick practice prompt asking students to identify why transactions between these two quantity levels do not occur, forcing them to articulate that the monopolist's artificial price premium blocks mutually beneficial trades where marginal benefit still exceeds marginal cost.

Finally, we formalize the concepts of allocative and productive efficiency. We explain that because the monopolist's price is strictly greater than marginal cost at the profit-maximizing quantity, the market fails allocative efficiency. We then direct attention to the average total cost curve to show that the monopolist does not produce at the minimum point of its ATC, thereby failing productive efficiency as well. This concludes the whiteboard sequence, leaving students with a clear graphical and conceptual understanding of why unchecked market power leads to market failure, setting them up perfectly for future policy interventions.

tasks: Locate and shade the deadweight loss area on a standard monopoly graph.
Compare the price and quantity of a monopoly with those of a perfectly competitive industry.

lectures.title: Pricing and Product Differentiation
lectures.description: Examine how firms segment markets through price discrimination and explore monopolistic competition in the short and long run.

sessions.title: Price Discrimination
sessions.description: Define price discrimination and model perfect (first-degree) price discrimination, showing its effect on consumer surplus, output, and deadweight loss.
sessions.sessionOutline:
Begin the session by introducing the intuitive concept of charging different prices to different customers. Rather than diving straight into math, ask the students to picture a movie theater: why do seniors and students pay less than working adults for the exact same seat and film? This opens the door to defining price discrimination as the business practice of selling the same good at different prices to different customers based on their willingness to pay. Emphasize that this is not about differences in production costs; if a premium version of a product costs more to make, charging a higher price is simply cost-plus pricing, not price discrimination. To pull off this strategy, a firm must satisfy three strict conditions, which should be clearly listed and discussed on the whiteboard: the firm must possess market power (price-setting ability), it must be able to segregate consumers based on their varying price elasticities of demand, and it must prevent resale (arbitrage) so that low-price buyers cannot instantly flip the product to high-value buyers.

Next, contrast this behavior with our standard benchmark on the whiteboard: the single-price monopolist. Draw the standard downward-sloping Demand curve and its corresponding Marginal Revenue (MR) curve, which lies below Demand. Walk through the logic of why MR is lower than price—to sell an additional unit, a single-price monopolist must lower the price on all previous units sold. Mark the profit-maximizing output where MR equals Marginal Cost (MC), trace up to the Demand curve to find the price, and visually shade the resulting Consumer Surplus (the upper triangle) and Deadweight Loss (the inefficiency triangle on the right). This establishes the status quo where the monopolist restricts output and leaves money on the table, creating a clear visual reference point before introducing the perfect price discriminator.

Now, transition to modeling first-degree, or perfect, price discrimination. On a fresh section of the whiteboard, challenge the students to imagine what happens if the monopolist knows exactly what every single customer is willing to pay and can charge them that exact maximum price. In this scenario, the MR curve completely collapses into the Demand curve. Explain the core mathematical and logical reason: because the firm can charge each customer a unique price, it no longer has to lower the price for prior customers to sell more. Each additional unit sold yields revenue exactly equal to the price paid for that unit. Therefore, the price on the Demand curve is the Marginal Revenue, leading to a single, downward-sloping line labeled 'D = MR'.

Guide students through the implications of this shift on quantity, surplus, and efficiency. Since the firm will produce as long as marginal revenue is greater than or equal to marginal cost, it will continue producing all the way to the point where the Demand curve intersects the Marginal Cost curve. Mark this new quantity on the whiteboard and point out that this is identical to the allocatively efficient output achieved under perfect competition. However, the distribution of surplus is radically different. Because every consumer is charged their exact maximum willingness to pay, Consumer Surplus is completely reduced to zero. The entire region that used to be Consumer Surplus, along with what used to be Deadweight Loss, is captured by the firm as Producer Surplus. 

Conclude by addressing a common AP Microeconomics pitfall: many students assume that because a monopoly is perfectly price-discriminating, the market must be highly inefficient. Clarify that while this outcome is highly unequal and unfavorable to consumers, it is technically 100% efficient from a societal standpoint because Deadweight Loss is eliminated and total surplus is maximized. Use a quick whiteboard practice task to cement this understanding: have students visually partition and compare the total surplus, consumer surplus, and deadweight loss between the single-price monopoly and the perfectly price-discriminating monopoly. This visual comparison guarantees they understand that while equity decreases, economic efficiency actually reaches its theoretical maximum.

tasks: Identify the three conditions necessary for price discrimination.
Compare the consumer surplus and deadweight loss of a perfectly price-discriminating monopolist to a single-price monopolist.

sessions.title: Monopolistic Competition in the Short Run
sessions.description: Describe the features of monopolistic competition and analyze its short-run pricing and output decisions using graphs showing economic profits or losses.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin this session by transitioning from the extreme model of pure monopoly to a highly realistic market structure that students encounter every single day: Monopolistic Competition. To ground this concept, invite students to think about their local neighborhood options for buying a cup of coffee or a slice of pizza. There are many competitors, and entry into the market is relatively easy, yet each establishment offers a slightly unique experience, taste, or brand identity. This element of product differentiation is the critical bridge; unlike perfect competition where products are identical and firms are price takers, monopolistically competitive firms possess a downward-sloping demand curve. This means they have some degree of price-making power. On the whiteboard, clearly outline the core characteristics of this market structure: many sellers, differentiated products, low barriers to entry and exit, and non-price competition. It is vital to emphasize that because these products are close but imperfect substitutes, the demand curve facing an individual firm is highly elastic but not perfectly flat.

Next, transition to drawing the short-run decision-making diagram on the whiteboard, walking students step-by-step through the logic of price and output determination. Draw a downward-sloping Demand curve and a Marginal Revenue (MR) curve that lies below it. Students must understand why MR lies below demand: to sell an additional unit of a differentiated product, the firm must lower the price on all previous units. Introduce the marginal cost (MC) curve as a standard U-shape. Demonstrate the universal profit-maximization rule where the firm produces at the quantity where MR equals MC. A frequent student pitfall is stopping at the intersection of MR and MC to find the price; make sure to physically draw a vertical dashed line from the MR=MC intersection up to the Demand curve to pinpoint the profit-maximizing price. Explain that this represents the maximum price consumers are willing to pay for that specific quantity of differentiated goods.

Now, layer the Average Total Cost (ATC) curve onto the whiteboard to analyze economic profit. Position the ATC curve such that at the profit-maximizing quantity, the ATC is lower than the price. This gap between the price and ATC represents the profit per unit. Shade in the resulting rectangle of positive economic profit, defined by the height (Price minus ATC) multiplied by the width (Quantity). Explain the intuitive economic meaning of this region: in the short run, unique branding, superior location, or a clever advertising campaign allows the firm to capture value above its opportunity costs. Contrast this with a scenario of short-run economic loss by illustrating a higher ATC curve, emphasizing that firms can indeed suffer losses if their differentiation fails to attract sufficient demand to cover average costs.

Conclude the whiteboard session by examining how firms actively maintain or increase this short-run profit through non-price competition. Ask the class what methods a business can use to convince customers that their product is superior to rivals. Discuss physical product differences, quality of service, location convenience, and heavily emphasized advertising campaigns. Illustrate on the board how successful differentiation shifts the firm's demand curve to the right and makes it more inelastic, allowing them to charge a higher price. To check for understanding, present a quick practice scenario: ask students to identify what would happen to the short-run profit diagram if a competitor opened next door with an identical advertising budget. This sets up a deep conceptual appreciation for how short-run dynamics trigger the entry and exit forces that lead to long-run equilibrium.

tasks: Graph a monopolistically competitive firm making a short-run economic profit.
List methods firms use to differentiate their products and increase demand.

sessions.title: Monopolistic Competition in the Long Run
sessions.description: Explain how free entry and exit lead to zero economic profit in the long run for monopolistic competition. Discuss excess capacity and efficiency.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin by bridging the gap between the short run and the long run in monopolistically competitive markets. Using a concept-first, public-lecture style, we start with an intuitive question: What happens when a new, trendy burger joint opens and starts making massive profits? Naturally, other entrepreneurs notice, and because barriers to entry are low, new competitors flood the neighborhood. This simple dynamic of free entry and exit is the driving force of the long-run transition. On the whiteboard, we illustrate this logic chain: short-run economic profits attract new entrants, which increases the variety of products available to consumers. As a result, the demand curve for any individual existing firm shifts to the left and becomes more elastic because consumers have more close substitutes. Conversely, if firms face short-run losses, some will exit, shifting the remaining firms' demand curves to the right. This self-correcting process only stops when economic profits are squeezed to exactly zero.

Next, we transition to the visual representation of this long-run equilibrium, which is one of the most challenging graphs in AP Microeconomics. On the whiteboard, we carefully construct the final equilibrium state. The core mathematical and logical constraint is that zero economic profit means Price (P) must equal Average Total Cost (ATC). Since the firm always maximizes profit where Marginal Revenue (MR) equals Marginal Cost (MC), this equality must occur at the profit-maximizing quantity. Thus, the demand curve must be tangent to the ATC curve at the exact quantity where MR intersects MC. We draw this step-by-step, showing how the ATC curve sits just above the demand curve everywhere except at that single point of tangency, representing zero economic profit.

We must actively address a classic student misconception during this graphing demonstration: many students mistakenly assume that because the firm is making zero economic profit, it must be producing at the minimum point of its ATC curve, just like a perfectly competitive firm. We visually debunk this on the board. Because the monopolistically competitive firm has market power, its demand curve is downward-sloping. A downward-sloping line can only be tangent to a U-shaped ATC curve on its downward-sloping segment, to the left of the minimum ATC. This means the firm does not produce at the lowest possible per-unit cost, which directly introduces the concept of productive inefficiency.

From this graphical realization, we define and label 'Excess Capacity.' We show that the gap between the firm's profit-maximizing output (where MR = MC) and its productively efficient output (where ATC is minimized) is the excess capacity. Conceptually, we explain this as the underutilization of resources: the firm has the physical capability to produce more output at a lower average cost, but it chooses not to because doing so would require lowering the price on all units, reducing marginal revenue below marginal cost. We also identify allocative inefficiency on the graph by showing that at the profit-maximizing quantity, the price consumers are willing to pay (on the demand curve) is greater than the marginal cost of production (P > MC), resulting in deadweight loss for society.

To wrap up the session, we conduct a structured graphing practice. We guide students through the precise order of operations for drawing this complex diagram from scratch, which is highly tested on the AP exam. We instruct them to draw the downward-sloping Demand and MR curves first, then the tick-mark of MC to establish the quantity, and finally to anchor the ATC curve so that its lowest point is to the right of the quantity line, while ensuring the curve itself is tangent to the demand curve directly above the MR=MC intersection. This sequence prevents the common graphical alignment errors that lead to lost points on FRQs.

tasks: Graph a monopolistically competitive firm in long-run equilibrium (tangency of demand and ATC).
Identify and explain the 'excess capacity' region on the firm's long-run graph.

lectures.title: Oligopoly and Strategic Behavior
lectures.description: Examine strategic interactions in oligopolistic markets, introducing game theory, Nash equilibria, and the incentives for collusion.

sessions.title: Oligopoly and Interdependence
sessions.description: Define oligopoly and strategic interdependence. Explain how concentration ratios are used to measure market power in these highly consolidated industries.
sessions.sessionOutline:
To begin this unit on imperfect competition, we introduce the concept of Oligopoly by drawing a sharp contrast to the highly fragmented markets students have seen so far. We set the stage by asking the class to think about the market for mobile phone operating systems or commercial aircraft. On the whiteboard, we map out a spectrum of market structures, placing Perfect Competition at one extreme, Monopoly at the other, and Oligopoly near the monopoly end. The core idea to establish immediately is that an oligopoly is characterized by a market dominated by a handfull of massive firms. This dominance creates a unique economic environment where the actions of one firm directly and powerfully impact the others, a defining characteristic known as strategic interdependence. Unlike a perfectly competitive firm that takes the market price as given, or a monopolist that acts without worrying about competitors, an oligopolist must constantly play a game of chess, anticipating the countermoves of its rivals.

Next, we list and explain the defining characteristics of an oligopoly on the board. We emphasize that these markets have high barriers to entry—such as massive capital requirements, brand loyalty, or control of key resources—which prevent new entrants from eroding the supernormal profits of the dominant firms. We also clarify that the products offered can be either homogeneous (like steel or oil) or highly differentiated (like automobiles or smartphones). The most critical point to emphasize here is 'mutual interdependence.' To help students internalize this, we present a scenario: if Firm A lowers its price, what happens to Firm B's market share? This naturally leads to the understanding that because firms are highly sensitive to their rivals' pricing and advertising strategies, they cannot make decisions in a vacuum.

To quantify this market power, we introduce the Four-Firm Concentration Ratio on the whiteboard. This tool measures the percentage of total industry sales accounted for by the four largest firms in the market. We write down the general formula: the sum of the market shares of the top four firms. We address a common misconception here: students often mistakenly believe that a high concentration ratio automatically proves a market is a monopoly, or they forget to sort the firms by market share before summing the top four. We walk through a clear example on the board, listing five hypothetical firms with market shares of 40%, 25%, 15%, 12%, and 8%. We demonstrate how to identify and sum the top four (40 + 25 + 15 + 12 = 92%) to show that this industry is highly concentrated, signifying an oligopolistic structure where a few players hold dominant market power.

To wrap up the session and verify understanding, we present a quick practice scenario. We ask the students to determine the four-firm concentration ratio of a market with six firms having market shares of 30%, 5%, 25%, 10%, 20%, and 10%. This exercise forces them to first rearrange the market shares in descending order (30%, 25%, 20%, 10%, 10%, 5%) before selecting and summing the top four. This practice highlights the mechanical pitfall of simply summing the first four numbers presented. Once the correct ratio of 85% is calculated, we lead a brief discussion on what this number means in real-world policy terms, signaling that the industry is ripe for strategic behavior and setting up the transition to game theory in the next session.

tasks: State the key characteristics of an oligopoly.
Calculate the four-firm concentration ratio from market share data.

sessions.title: Game Theory and Payoff Matrices
sessions.description: Introduce game theory terminology (players, strategies, payoffs) and construct a standard 2x2 payoff matrix representing strategic interaction.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin this session by transitioning from the structural characteristics of oligopoly to the analytical tool used to study them: Game Theory. Because oligopolistic firms are highly interdependent, their profits depend not just on their own pricing or marketing actions, but crucially on the actions of their competitors. To make sense of this interactive environment, we introduce the three fundamental pillars of any game: players, strategies, and payoffs. It is vital to emphasize to students that 'players' in microeconomics are usually competing firms, 'strategies' represent their operational choices (such as charging a high versus low price, or launching a massive advertising campaign), and 'payoffs' represent the resulting economic outcomes, typically measured in profit or revenue.

Next, we introduce the visual engine of this analysis: the standard 2x2 payoff matrix. On the whiteboard, draw a clear, large square divided into four distinct quadrants. Place 'Firm A' along the left-hand side representing the row player, and 'Firm B' along the top representing the column player. Clearly label the two strategies for each firm—for example, 'Advertise' and 'Do Not Advertise'. The core instructional challenge here is helping students navigate the coordinate system of payoffs. Use distinct colors on the whiteboard (e.g., blue for the row player and red for the column player) to write the numerical payoffs within each cell, separated by a comma (e.g., $10, $15). 

We must actively address a classic student misconception: confusing which number belongs to which firm. Explicitly teach the universal convention that the first number in any cell always belongs to the row player (the firm on the left), and the second number always belongs to the column player (the firm on top). A useful visual trick to demonstrate on the board is drawing arrows pointing from the respective player labels to their corresponding values within a single cell. Explain that a single cell represents a joint outcome—the intersection of one specific choice made by Firm A and one specific choice made by Firm B.

To solidify this layout, walk through a concrete business scenario. Suppose two rival food delivery apps are deciding whether to offer a promotional discount. If both discount, they split the market but earn lower profits. If only one discounts, that firm steals the market share, yielding high profits while the rival suffers a loss. If neither discounts, they maintain moderate profits. Map these real-world narratives into the cells on the board, cell by cell, asking students to identify which numbers go up or down based on the story. This practice moment forces students to translate descriptive business strategy into a formal economic model, ensuring they understand the payoff matrix as a live dynamic rather than a static grid of arbitrary numbers.

tasks: Interpret the payoffs in a given 2x2 matrix for both players.
Map real-world business decisions (e.g., pricing, advertising) into a game theory matrix.

sessions.title: Dominant Strategies and Nash Equilibrium
sessions.description: Solve a payoff matrix to identify dominant strategies, dominated strategies, and find the Nash equilibrium (or equilibria) of a game.
sessions.sessionOutline:
Begin the session by transitioning from the structural layout of a game theory matrix to the actual decision-making process. State the central question of strategic behavior: in a world of mutual interdependence where your rival's choice directly affects your outcome, how do you make a rational decision? Introduce the whiteboard by sketching a clean 2x2 matrix representing two competing firms, Firm A (Row Player) and Firm B (Column Player), deciding between 'High Price' and 'Low Price'. Emphasize that before doing any math, students must master the coordinate reading rule: the first payoff belongs to the Row player, and the second payoff belongs to the Column player. A classic student error is swapping these values during analysis, which completely invalidates the equilibrium search.

Define the concept of a dominant strategy as the holy grail of strategic decision-making. Explain that a dominant strategy is an action that yields a strictly higher payoff than any other strategy, regardless of what the opponent chooses to do. To visualize this on the whiteboard, cover up Firm B's column for 'Low Price' with your hand, forcing students to look only at 'High Price' and compare Firm A's payoffs. Then, swap and cover the 'High Price' column. Walk through this logical check step-by-step: 'If Firm B chooses High, Firm A should choose X. If Firm B chooses Low, Firm A should still choose X.' When the optimal choice remains identical under all circumstances, Firm A has a dominant strategy. Conversely, define a dominated strategy as an option that is always worse, which rational players can immediately cross off their list to simplify their cognitive load.

Now, pivot to situations where one or both players do not possess a dominant strategy, which introduces the need for the Nash Equilibrium. Define Nash Equilibrium conceptually as a state of mutual best responses where no player has an incentive to unilaterally deviate from their chosen action. Frame this as a 'state of no regrets'—if the game is played and the players look at the resulting cell, neither would wish they had chosen differently given what the other player actually did. 

Introduce the 'Underline Method' as a foolproof, highly visual diagnostic tool on the whiteboard. For the Row player (Firm A), look down each column (representing Firm B's choices) individually, identify Firm A's highest payoff in that column, and draw a firm underline under that first number. Next, shift perspective to the Column player (Firm B): look across each row (representing Firm A's choices) individually, identify Firm B's highest payoff in that row, and underline that second number. Explain that any cell containing two underlined payoffs represents a Nash Equilibrium. This visual technique prevents students from getting lost in mental calculations and ensures accuracy under high-stress exam conditions.

Address key misconceptions before concluding. Explain that a Nash Equilibrium does not necessarily mean the players are happy, nor does it mean they have maximized their joint profits. Use the classic Prisoner's Dilemma payoffs to show how both players ended up in a Nash Equilibrium that yields lower profits than if they had cooperated, illustrating the tragic tension between individual rationality and collective welfare. Additionally, warn students that a game can have two Nash equilibria, or even none in pure strategies. Wrap up by writing a fresh payoff matrix on the board and having students independently apply the underline method to find the Nash equilibrium, demonstrating their mastery of strategic derivation.

tasks: Determine if a player has a dominant strategy in a given matrix.
Identify the Nash equilibrium from a matrix using the underline method.

sessions.title: Collusion and Strategic Competition
sessions.description: Analyze the cooperative outcome of collusion (cartels) and explain why the prisoner's dilemma creates a strong incentive for firms to cheat on cartels.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin this whiteboard session by transitioning from the static, one-shot games analyzed previously to the dynamic, real-world interactions of oligopoly firms. The central question of this session is why firms in highly concentrated markets, which could earn monopoly-like profits by working together, so often end up in price wars or aggressive competition. On the whiteboard, draw a large circle representing the 'Monopoly Profit Pie' and divide it into two equal halves to represent a duopoly. Explain that collusion occurs when firms formally or informally agree to restrict their collective output and raise prices to secure this monopoly outcome. When this agreement is formal and binding, we call it a cartel. 

Next, we expose the inherent instability of this cooperative agreement using a standard prisoner's dilemma framework. On the whiteboard, construct a 2x2 payoff matrix representing two firms, Firm A and Firm B, choosing between 'Cooperate' (abide by the agreed high price/restricted output) and 'Cheat' (underprice the rival or overproduce). Populate the matrix with numbers that demonstrate that if both cooperate, they split the high monopoly profit. However, if Firm A cheats while Firm B cooperates, Firm A captures almost the entire market, earning a massive profit while Firm B suffers a loss. Because both firms face the same payoff structure, each has a dominant strategy to cheat. Walk through the logic step-by-step: no matter what the rival does, cheating yields a higher individual payoff in the short run. The Nash equilibrium lands squarely in the bottom-right quadrant where both cheat, resulting in lower profits for both than if they had successfully colluded. This reveals the core economic tension: collective rationality dictates cooperation, but individual rationality drives both to cheat.

A common student misconception is that cartels are primarily broken up by government regulators or antitrust authorities. While laws do play a massive role, the teacher must emphasize that cartels are fundamentally self-destructive due to this economic incentive structure. To prevent this misunderstanding, write the phrase 'Internal Instability vs. External Regulation' on the board, and prompt students to articulate how a cartel could fall apart even in a completely unregulated market.

To bridge this grim outcome to reality, introduce the concept of repeated games. In the real world, firms do not interact just once; they face each other day after day, year after year. This repetition transforms the strategic landscape. Introduce the 'grim trigger' strategy and the 'tit-for-tat' strategy on the whiteboard. Explain how the threat of future retaliation can punish a cheating firm so severely in subsequent rounds that the short-term gains from cheating are completely wiped out. Under a grim trigger strategy, if one firm cheats once, the other cooperates no longer and wages a permanent price war. Under tit-for-tat, a firm mimics its rival's previous move. This makes cooperation self-enforcing because the shadow of the future outweighs the temptation of the present.

Conclude the session with a practice prompt asking students to analyze a scenario where two major airlines are tempted to lower ticket prices. Students should explain, first, why a one-shot game leads to a low-fare equilibrium, and second, how the expectation of daily, repeated flights on the same route allows them to maintain high fares without explicit, illegal communication. This exercise forces students to apply the abstract concepts of repeated games and threats to concrete business strategy, solidifying their understanding of oligopoly behavior.

tasks: Explain why cartels are unstable over time using game theory concepts.
Explain how repeated games and threat strategies can support cooperative behavior.

units.title: Factor Markets
units.description: Investigate how firms demand inputs (labor, capital) and how resource prices are determined in competitive and monopsonistic resource markets.

lectures.title: Factor Demand and Supply
lectures.description: Introduce the fundamentals of input markets, focusing on how firms decide how many resources to hire based on productivity and demand for the final product.

sessions.title: Factor Markets and Derived Demand
sessions.description: Define factor markets and explain why the demand for resources is a 'derived demand' based on the demand for the goods they produce.
sessions.sessionOutline:
Begin the lecture by drawing a simplified Circular Flow Model on the whiteboard to ground the students in familiar territory before flipping their perspective. Clearly label the two primary sectors—Households and Firms—and the two key arenas of interaction—Product Markets and Factor (Resource) Markets. Remind students that throughout Units 1 through 4, they analyzed the Product Market, where households act as buyers and firms act as sellers. Now, draw bold, contrasting arrows to illustrate the fundamental role reversal that occurs in Factor Markets: here, households own the factors of production (labor, land, capital, and entrepreneurship) and act as the suppliers, while firms act as the demanders, purchasing these resources to fuel their production. Explicitly warn students against the classic pitfall of assuming households are always the buyers; in this unit, firms are the ones spending money to acquire inputs.

Once this market structure is established, introduce the concept of 'derived demand' as the central theme of resource markets. Write the term in large letters on the board and define it not just as a formal vocabulary word, but as a chain of causality: the demand for any input is derived entirely from the demand for the final output that the input helps produce. To make this intuitive, use the example of a local bakery. A bakery does not hire bakers because it simply wants to employ people; it hires them because consumers want to buy bread. If consumer demand for bread vanishes, the bakery's demand for bakers instantly disappears, regardless of how skilled the bakers are. Use this to establish that factor demand is a secondary, dependent demand.

Translate this conceptual link into a side-by-side graphical demonstration on the whiteboard. On the left side, draw a standard supply and demand graph for a consumer good, such as specialty coffee, showing an initial market equilibrium. On the right side, draw the resource market for coffee baristas, with wage on the vertical axis and quantity of labor on the horizontal axis. Walk through a scenario where a new health study or social trend dramatically increases the consumer demand for specialty coffee. Shift the coffee demand curve to the right, showing an increase in both market price and quantity. Immediately draw a physical arrow pointing from the new, higher equilibrium price of coffee on the left graph across the board to the barista market on the right graph. Explain that because coffee is now more valuable and highly demanded, the labor that produces it becomes more valuable to the firm, causing the demand curve for baristas to shift to the right as well.

Conclude the session with a brief conceptual checkpoint designed to reinforce this transmission mechanism and head off common misunderstandings. Ask the students to consider a reverse scenario, such as a sudden decline in the popularity of print newspapers, and trace how this affects the employment market for newspaper printing press operators. Use this prompt to ensure students can confidently articulate the multi-step chain of events: a drop in product demand leads to a drop in product price and quantity, which directly reduces the economic value of the workers' output, ultimately causing a leftward shift in the demand curve for those specific workers.

tasks: Distinguish between product markets and factor markets.
Explain how an increase in demand for a final product shifts the demand curve for the labor that produces it.

sessions.title: Marginal Revenue Product and Marginal Resource Cost
sessions.description: Formulate and calculate Marginal Revenue Product (MRP) and Marginal Resource Cost (MRC), establishing the hiring rule where MRP equals MRC.
sessions.sessionOutline:
Begin the session by connecting the student's existing knowledge of product markets to the input market. On the whiteboard, draw a clear parallel: just as a firm maximizes profit by producing where Marginal Revenue equals Marginal Cost (MR = MC), a firm also maximizes profit by hiring inputs where the marginal benefit of that input equals its marginal cost. Introduce the core question of this session: 'How does a business owner decide whether to hire one more worker?' This transitions the discussion from physical units of output to financial values of inputs.

Define Marginal Revenue Product (MRP) conceptually before writing any equations. Explain that MRP represents the additional revenue a firm earns by employing one more unit of a resource. To make this intuitive, draw a two-step logical chain on the whiteboard: hiring a worker first increases physical production—which is the Marginal Product (MP)—and selling that additional output in the product market converts those units into dollars. Write the formula MRP = MP × Price (for a perfectly competitive product market) and emphasize that MRP is downward sloping primarily due to the Law of Diminishing Marginal Returns, not because the product price is falling.

Next, introduce the cost side by defining Marginal Resource Cost (MRC). Explain that MRC is the additional cost incurred by employing one more unit of a resource. Since we are assuming a perfectly competitive labor market, the firm is a 'wage-taker' and can hire as many workers as it wants at the market-determined wage. Draw a horizontal line on the whiteboard and label it MRC = Wage. Address a common student pitfall here: students often confuse the product price (from the product market) with the wage rate (from the labor market). Clearly distinguish that the wage is what the firm pays the worker, while the product price is what the firm receives when selling the goods the worker produced.

Walk through a complete numerical example on the whiteboard. Create a four-column schedule: Labor (0 to 5), Total Product of pies, Product Price (fixed at $10), and Wage (fixed at $20). Have the teacher calculate the physical Marginal Product (MP) for each worker first, then calculate the Marginal Revenue Product (MRP) by multiplying MP by the $10 price. Next, fill in the MRC column, which remains a constant $20 for every worker. Guide the students through the decision-making process for each sequential worker. For example, if the second worker's MRP is $30 and their MRC is $20, the firm should hire them because they add more to revenue than to costs. Show that the firm will continue hiring until the MRP of the last worker is equal to (or just greater than) the MRC.

Conclude by sketching the graphical equilibrium of the firm's hiring decision on the whiteboard. Plot the downward-sloping MRP curve (which is the firm's labor demand curve) and the horizontal MRC curve (the firm's labor supply curve). Mark the intersection point to show the profit-maximizing quantity of labor. Warn students against a common AP exam trap: if MRP is less than MRC for a particular worker, hiring that worker actually reduces the firm's total profit. The goal is not to maximize total output or total revenue, but to maximize net profit by stopping exactly where the marginal benefit of labor equals its marginal cost.

tasks: Calculate MRP and MRC from schedules of labor inputs, physical outputs, and product prices.
Graph MRP and MRC for a perfectly competitive firm in the labor market.

sessions.title: Changes in Factor Demand and Supply
sessions.description: Analyze the determinants of resource demand (product price, productivity, prices of other resources) and resource supply (demographics, preferences, alternatives).
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin this session by transitioning from the static derivation of Marginal Revenue Product (MRP) to a dynamic environment where the factor demand and supply curves shift. The main objective is to help students understand that factor demand is a derived demand, which means any change in the product market directly alters the resource market. To illustrate this on the whiteboard, draw a side-by-side graph of a product market (like coffee cups) and the labor market for baristas. Explain that if a sudden fitness trend increases the demand for coffee, the market price of coffee rises. Because $MRP = MP \times P$, this rise in product price ($P$) immediately shifts the labor demand curve (the $MRP$ curve) to the right, even if the physical productivity of the baristas remains completely unchanged. This logic chain is crucial: changes in consumer tastes for a final good alter its price, which in turn alters the marginal value of the labor that makes it.

Next, introduce productivity as the second major shifter of resource demand. On the whiteboard, define how technological advancements or training alter the Marginal Product ($MP$) of labor. Use the example of introducing high-speed automated espresso machines. This technology allows each barista to produce more cups of coffee per hour, increasing their marginal product. As $MP$ rises, the $MRP$ curve shifts to the right, increasing the firm's demand for skilled labor. However, warn teachers about a classic AP Microeconomics trap: the distinction between technology as a complement versus technology as a substitute. If a new technology completely replaces workers (like a fully automated self-service coffee kiosk), the demand for unskilled labor will shift to the left because capital is substituting for labor. Walk teachers through drawing these two distinct scenarios to ensure students do not falsely assume that 'technology always increases labor demand.'

We then shift our focus to the supply side of the factor market, exploring what causes the labor supply curve to shift. Draw a standard upward-sloping labor supply curve on the board and introduce the determinants: demographics, societal preferences, and alternative opportunities. To make this concrete, ask the students to imagine a scenario where a new, high-paying tech campus opens up next door to our coffee shops, offering entry-level administrative jobs with better hours and higher pay. This alternative employment opportunity increases the opportunity cost of working as a barista, causing the supply of baristas to shift to the left. Teachers should emphasize that labor supply is not fixed; it is highly sensitive to the relative attractiveness, safety, and non-monetary benefits of alternative jobs.

Conclude the session with an active learning practice moment designed to test these shifting dynamics. Present students with a scenario: 'The government subsidizes training programs for software developers, while simultaneously, a global shortage of silicon chips drives up the price of software.' Ask students to analyze how these two concurrent events shift the demand and supply for software engineers, and what the net effect will be on equilibrium wages. This practice exercise is designed to reveal whether students can distinguish between a shift in supply (caused by the training subsidy increasing the pool of qualified workers) and a shift in demand (caused by the higher product price increasing $MRP$). By tracing both shifts on a single whiteboard graph, students will visually grasp how market forces interact to establish new equilibrium wages.

tasks: Predict how a change in technology shifts the demand for skilled and unskilled labor.
Determine how alternative employment opportunities affect labor supply in a specific market.

sessions.title: Factor-Market Equilibrium
sessions.description: Combine resource demand and resource supply curves to find equilibrium wages and employment in a perfectly competitive market.
sessions.sessionOutline:
Begin the session by connecting the previous discussions on individual firm demand and supply to the broader market context. Introduce the concept of a dual-graph setup on the whiteboard, positioning the market for labor on the left and a single representative firm on the right. Explain that while we have analyzed how a single firm calculates its Marginal Revenue Product (MRP) to make hiring decisions, that firm does not operate in a vacuum; it must accept the wage rate determined by the collective actions of all employers and workers in the market. This sets up the concept of the firm as a 'wage taker' in a perfectly competitive factor market.

Draw the market graph on the left with a standard downward-sloping labor demand curve (representing the sum of all firms' MRP curves) and an upward-sloping labor supply curve (representing the aggregate choices of households). Mark the intersection to establish the market equilibrium wage and the total quantity of labor employed. Directly project this equilibrium wage horizontally across the board to the firm's graph on the right. This visual link is crucial: it shows students that the market-clearing wage directly establishes the firm's perfectly elastic labor supply curve, which is identical to its Marginal Resource Cost (MRC). Emphasize that because the firm can hire as many workers as it wants at this market-clearing wage, its additional cost for hiring one more worker remains constant and equal to that wage.

Address a major AP microeconomics pitfall here: students frequently confuse the upward-sloping market labor supply curve with the individual firm's labor supply curve. To prevent this, guide students through a conceptual thought experiment. Ask them what would happen if a single small firm tried to pay a wage lower than the market rate (they would lose all their workers to competitors) or higher than the market rate (they would waste profits unnecessarily). This reinforces the logic of why the individual firm's labor supply curve is perfectly horizontal, even though the market-wide supply curve is upward-sloping.

Now, introduce a dynamic market shift to demonstrate the transmission mechanism. Suppose there is a sudden increase in the demand for the final product that these workers produce. Walk through the chain of causality: higher product demand increases the product price, which shifts the market demand for labor outward. On the whiteboard, draw the rightward shift of the market demand curve, which drives up the equilibrium wage rate. Consequently, show how this forces the individual firm's horizontal MRC curve to shift upward. The firm must now pay this higher wage to all workers, and as a result, its profit-maximizing hiring level (where the new MRC intersects its unchanged MRP) will decrease. This exercise helps students practice tracing changes from product markets to factor markets, and ultimately to the hiring decisions of individual firms.

tasks: Determine the equilibrium wage rate and employment level from market supply and demand schedules.
Explain how wage shifts affect a firm's MRC curve.

lectures.title: Competitive and Monopsonistic Markets
lectures.description: Compare hiring decisions in competitive labor markets to wage-setting behaviors in monopsonistic labor markets, assessing efficiency.

sessions.title: Profit Maximization in Competitive Factor Markets
sessions.description: Model a firm that is a price-taker in both the product market and the factor market, establishing the MRP=MRC hiring decision.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin this session by establishing the bridge between the product market and the factor market. The core objective is to transition students from thinking about a firm selling goods to thinking about a firm buying resources, specifically labor. To introduce this intuitively, we start with a real-world scenario of a local bakery operating in a perfectly competitive town. The bakery is a price-taker in both markets: it cannot influence the market price of croissants, nor can it influence the going wage rate for bakers. This double price-taker status is the foundation of our entire model. We will represent this on the whiteboard by drawing a parallel between the consumer's demand for goods and the firm's demand for inputs, highlighting that factor demand is a 'derived demand'—it only exists because there is demand for the final product the workers produce.

Next, we transition to the whiteboard to construct the classic side-by-side graphical model. On the left, we draw the industry or market for labor, showing a standard downward-sloping labor demand curve and an upward-sloping labor supply curve. The intersection of these curves establishes the market wage. We then draw the individual firm's graph on the right, directly projecting this market wage horizontally across to create a perfectly elastic labor supply curve for the firm, which represents the Marginal Resource Cost (MRC). A common pitfall for students is confusing the firm's labor supply with the market labor supply. We must explicitly point out that because the individual firm is tiny relative to the market, it can hire as many workers as it wants at that constant market wage, meaning its marginal cost of hiring one more worker is constant and equal to that wage.

Once the supply side of the labor market is established, we construct the demand side for the individual firm, introducing the concept of Marginal Revenue Product (MRP). We derive this by showing how each additional worker contributes to physical output (Marginal Product) and how that output is valued in the market (Marginal Revenue). Since our firm is a price-taker in the product market, MRP is simply Marginal Product multiplied by the product price. We draw the downward-sloping MRP curve on the firm's graph, explaining that its downward slope is driven entirely by the Law of Diminishing Marginal Returns. We must warn students against a classic AP misconception: the MRP curve does not slope downward because product price is falling (as in a monopoly), but because the physical productivity of additional workers eventually declines.

With both the MRP and MRC curves plotted on the firm's graph, we guide students to the fundamental profit-maximization decision rule: hire workers up to the point where MRP equals MRC. We walk through a numerical example on the board to illustrate this. If a worker's MRP is fifty dollars and the wage (MRC) is thirty dollars, hiring that worker adds twenty dollars to total profit. Conversely, if the next worker's MRP is twenty dollars and the wage is thirty dollars, hiring them would reduce profit. The logical stopping point is where the benefit of the last unit of labor matches its cost. Students will practice identifying this intersection on their own graphs, which serves as a powerful diagnostic tool to ensure they understand how the rule translates into a concrete employment quantity on the horizontal axis.

tasks: Draw side-by-side graphs of a competitive labor market and a firm hiring labor from that market.
Determine the profit-maximizing quantity of workers to hire for a price-taking firm.

sessions.title: Wage and Employment Decisions in a Monopsony
sessions.description: Define monopsony and explain why a monopsonist faces an upward-sloping labor supply curve, making its MRC higher than the wage rate. Analyze monopsonistic exploitation.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin by introducing the concept of a monopsony, translating its Greek roots—'single buyer'—into a concrete, intuitive scenario: the classic company town where a single coal mine or manufacturing plant is the sole employer. Unlike a perfectly competitive firm that can hire as many workers as it wants at the market-clearing wage, a monopsonist is the market. This structural shift is crucial because it means the firm faces the entire upward-sloping market supply curve for labor. To hire more workers, the monopsonist cannot simply accept a market wage; they must raise the wage rate to attract additional labor. This sets the stage for our core analytical puzzle.

Next, we derive why the Marginal Resource Cost (MRC) curve must lie above the wage rate (the Supply curve). Using the whiteboard, we construct a simple numerical table. If hiring 1 worker costs $10, total labor cost is $10. To hire a second worker, the firm must offer $11. Crucially, due to non-discriminating wage laws, the firm must pay *both* workers $11, raising the total cost to $22. The marginal cost of that second worker is not just their own wage ($11), but $12—the new wage plus the $1 raise given to the first worker. On the whiteboard, we plot these points to visually demonstrate that the MRC curve rises at twice the slope of the Supply curve. We must explicitly warn students against the common pitfall of confusing the supply curve of labor with the marginal resource cost curve; they are distinct functions whenever a firm has wage-setting power.

With both curves graphed, we locate the profit-maximizing hiring point where Marginal Revenue Product (MRP) equals MRC. The whiteboard illustration shows the intersection of MRP and MRC, projecting down to establish the profit-maximizing quantity of labor, Q_m. However, the biggest trap for AP students lies in finding the wage. Students often project horizontally to the intersection, but we must guide them to look down at the labor supply curve at quantity Q_m to find the actual wage paid, W_m. Since workers are willing to work for W_m at quantity Q_m, the firm will only pay W_m, which is significantly lower than the worker's MRP.

We conclude by analyzing 'monopsonistic exploitation' and market inefficiency. By comparing the monopsony outcome (Q_m, W_m) to the socially optimal competitive outcome where Supply equals Demand (MRP), we highlight the deadweight loss triangle. The gap between the worker's marginal contribution to revenue (MRP) and the actual wage paid (W_m) represents the economic rent captured by the employer at the expense of labor. We will run a quick practice checkpoint where students must shade this deadweight loss area and identify the specific coordinates of exploitation, solidifying their understanding of why a monopsony leads to underemployment and lower wages compared to a competitive benchmark.

tasks: Graph a monopsonistic labor market, showing why the MRC curve lies above the labor supply curve.
Identify the wage and employment level of a monopsonistic firm on a graph.

sessions.title: Minimum Wages in Competitive and Monopsonistic Markets
sessions.description: Compare the microeconomic impacts of a government-mandated minimum wage in a perfectly competitive labor market versus a monopsony.
sessions.sessionOutline:
Begin the session by framing a classic economic paradox: while standard economic theory predicts that setting a minimum wage above equilibrium creates a surplus of labor (unemployment), real-world empirical data sometimes shows employment rising after a minimum wage hike. Explain that this session will resolve this paradox by analyzing how market structure dictates policy outcomes. This contrast is not just a favorite AP Microeconomics topic, but a fundamental lesson in why policy analysis must always start with an understanding of market power.

On the whiteboard, first draw a perfectly competitive labor market in equilibrium, labeling the intersection of labor demand (MRP) and labor supply at wage Wc and employment Lc. Then, introduce a binding minimum wage, Wmin, above the equilibrium wage. Guide the teacher to visually trace how this floor creates a wedge. At Wmin, the quantity of labor supplied by workers increases to Ls, while the quantity of labor demanded by firms contracts to Ld. The difference (Ls - Ld) represents a surplus of labor, which translates directly to unemployment. Emphasize to students that because competitive firms are price-takers, they have no power over the wage and must reduce hiring to keep marginal revenue product equal to this new, higher marginal resource cost.

Transition to the monopsony model, where a single employer faces the entire upward-sloping labor supply curve and must pay a higher wage to all existing workers to attract an additional worker, making its Marginal Resource Cost (MRC) curve lie strictly above the supply curve. Remind students that the unregulated monopsonist restricts employment to Lm and pays a wage of Wm, which is below both the competitive wage and the marginal revenue product of the last worker. This difference represents monopsonistic exploitation and deadweight loss. Explain that a government-mandated minimum wage completely changes the marginal incentives of this single buyer.

Demonstrate the graphical transformation on the whiteboard step-by-step. When a minimum wage, Wmin, is set above Wm (but below the intersection of MRC and MRP), the monopsonist can no longer pay Wm. For any quantity of labor up to where Wmin hits the labor supply curve, the marginal cost of hiring an additional worker is simply Wmin, because the firm no longer has to raise wages for all previous workers to recruit another—the wage is already legally fixed at Wmin. This turns the labor supply curve, and consequently the MRC curve, completely horizontal at the level of the minimum wage. The teacher should trace this new, flat MRC line and show where it intersects the MRP curve. This intersection yields a higher quantity of labor hired than the unregulated monopsony level, effectively showing that the minimum wage forces the monopsonist to behave more like a perfect competitor.

Warn teachers about the primary student pitfall: the 'jump' or discontinuity in the new MRC curve. Students often get confused about what happens to the MRC curve once employment exceeds the point where Wmin meets the original supply curve. Explain that at that boundary point, the firm must revert to the original upward-sloping supply curve to hire more workers, causing the MRC to jump vertically back up to the original MRC curve. Conclude with a targeted whiteboard drawing practice where students must illustrate this discontinuity and identify the optimal range for a minimum wage that simultaneously maximizes employment and minimizes deadweight loss.

tasks: Graph how a binding minimum wage creates unemployment in a competitive labor market.
Demonstrate graphically how a minimum wage can actually increase employment in a monopsonistic labor market.
